title: The Future of Peer Review
text:
Peer review remains the principal mechanism through which academic journals assess the validity of submitted research. In a typical process, an editor selects several independent experts who evaluate the manuscript's methodology, originality and significance before recommending acceptance, revision or rejection. Although the system is widely regarded as essential for maintaining scholarly rigour, critics argue that its anonymity can conceal bias and that reviewers are often overburdened.

In response, some journals have experimented with open peer review, in which reviewers' identities and comments are published alongside the article. Early evidence suggests that this practice can make reviews more constructive, although it may also discourage candid criticism from junior researchers who fear reprisal. Consequently, many scholars now recommend hybrid models that combine transparency with confidentiality, a compromise whose long-term effects remain under investigation.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what is the role of an editor in peer review?
options: To publish the article without any review
To select independent experts to evaluate a manuscript
To write the final article themselves
To provide funding for the research

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do some journals do in open peer review?
options: They keep the reviewers' identities secret
They publish reviewers' identities and comments alongside the article

questions.text: What can be inferred about junior researchers in open peer review?
options: They are likely to welcome open criticism without any concern
They may hesitate to give candid criticism
They are never asked to review manuscripts
They always receive higher pay than senior reviewers

questions.text: What is the author's most likely attitude towards hybrid models?
options: Cautiously supportive, but aware that their long-term effects are unknown
Indifferent, because they have no practical value
Certain that they are clearly superior to all other systems

paragraph_translations: A revisão por pares continua a ser o principal mecanismo através do qual as revistas académicas avaliam a validade das pesquisas submetidas. Num processo típico, um editor seleciona vários especialistas independentes que avaliam a metodologia, a originalidade e a relevância do manuscrito antes de recomendar aceitação, revisão ou rejeição. Embora o sistema seja amplamente considerado essencial para manter o rigor académico, os críticos argumentam que o anonimato pode ocultar preconceitos e que os revisores estão frequentemente sobrecarregados.

Em resposta, algumas revistas experimentaram a revisão aberta, na qual as identidades e os comentários dos revisores são publicados junto com o artigo. As primeiras evidências sugerem que essa prática pode tornar as revisões mais construtivas, embora também possa desencorajar críticas francas por parte de investigadores juniores que temem represálias. Consequentemente, muitos académicos recomendam agora modelos híbridos que combinam transparência com confidencialidade, um compromisso cujos efeitos a longo prazo continuam a ser investigados.
